title: Major Art Movements
description: Western art movements from the Renaissance to Minimalism, each with its era, defining traits, and one artist to know.
subject: arts-humanities

cards.definition: Late 19th-century France. Loose, visible brushwork and everyday scenes, often painted outdoors to capture changing light. Artist: Claude Monet.
Early 20th century. Breaks subjects into geometric planes and shows several viewpoints at once. Artist: Pablo Picasso.
1920s onward. Dreamlike, irrational imagery meant to tap the unconscious mind. Artist: Salvador Dalí.
15th and 16th centuries. Revived classical ideals with linear perspective, realistic anatomy, and balanced composition. Artist: Leonardo da Vinci.
17th-century Europe. Dramatic contrasts of light and shadow, movement, and emotional intensity. Artist: Caravaggio.
18th-century France. Light, ornate, playful scenes in soft pastel colors. Artist: Jean-Honoré Fragonard.
Late 18th to early 19th century. Restrained, orderly works modeled on ancient Greece and Rome. Artist: Jacques-Louis David.
Late 18th to mid-19th century. Emotion and imagination over cool reason, and the overwhelming power of nature. Artist: Caspar David Friedrich.
Mid-19th-century France. Unidealized depictions of ordinary people and everyday life. Artist: Gustave Courbet.
Late 19th century. Built on Impressionism with bolder color, stronger form, and personal expression. Artist: Vincent van Gogh.
Around 1890 to 1910. Decorative style of flowing, organic lines inspired by plants and natural forms. Artist: Alphonse Mucha.
Early 1900s France. Wild, non-naturalistic color applied in bold, flat strokes. Artist: Henri Matisse.
Early 20th century, centered in Germany. Distorted forms and intense color used to convey inner emotion. Artist: Ernst Ludwig Kirchner.
Founded in Italy in 1909. Celebrated speed, machines, and modern life with dynamic, fragmented images of motion. Artist: Umberto Boccioni.
Began in 1916, during World War I. An anti-art movement that used absurdity and chance to mock convention. Artist: Marcel Duchamp.
Founded in the Netherlands in 1917. Pure abstraction using straight lines, right angles, and primary colors. Artist: Piet Mondrian.
German school, 1919 to 1933. Unified art, craft, and industrial design around simple, functional forms. Founder: architect Walter Gropius.
1940s and 1950s New York. Large-scale abstraction emphasizing spontaneous gesture or fields of color. Artist: Jackson Pollock.
Mid-1950s and 1960s, Britain and the US. Borrowed imagery from advertising, comics, and consumer products. Artist: Andy Warhol.
1960s. Simple geometric forms and industrial materials, stripped of personal expression. Artist: Donald Judd.
